aka: Countess Helene von Stein lamb's ear
origin: A garden selection of a species from the rocky hills of Turkey, the Caucasus and northern Iran
habitat: Wild ancestor grows on dry, stony hillsides and rocky slopes in full sun
blurb: The big-leaved lamb's ear, and the one that actually holds up. Its velvety tongue-shaped leaves reach 8 in — up to twice the length of the ordinary species — and they read grey-green rather than the species' bright silver-white. The trade-off is deliberate: 'Big Ears' almost never throws flower spikes, so it stays a clean unbroken carpet of foliage instead of going leggy and ratty at bloom time, and it never seeds itself around. It also shrugs off the rot and leaf-spot that disfigure ordinary lamb's ear in a damp season, which makes it the safest bet of the family for a Front Range bed that gets any overhead spray.
size: 8–12 in foliage mound × 1–2 ft wide; individual leaves to 8 in long
sun: Full sun; afternoon shade is welcome in the hottest, most reflective spots
water: Low; xeric once established — keep overhead spray off the wool, which traps water and rots
spread: Spreads by runners that root where the stems touch soil, knitting into a dense mat; it seldom flowers, so it does not self-sow
seasons: Grey-green woolly mound from spring through fall, at its best in cool spring growth; only rare, sporadic flower spikes; semi-evergreen — the mat persists through mild winters but flattens and browns in a hard one
wildlife: Wool carder bees (Anthidium spp.) shave the leaf fuzz to line their nest cells, so the foliage itself has value; because it so rarely blooms it offers little nectar compared with the ordinary species
deer: Deer and rabbit resistant — neither will touch the woolly foliage
toxic: Non-toxic to people and pets; not a culinary plant
gaps: Reel covers spring, summer and fall. No open-licensed winter photo of this cultivar exists — it is semi-evergreen but flattens and browns here, so a Front-Range winter shot would show a tattered grey mat rather than anything useful. Capped at good-plus for the seasonal axis.

care.hardiness: Hardy in USDA zones 4–9, so it is comfortably reliable across the Front Range (zones 5b–6a).[1][2] It stays evergreen through mild winters but dies back nearly to the ground where winters are cold, so expect a flattened, tattered mat by February here and fresh growth in spring.[2] The heavy leaf wool is the plant's own sunscreen — it reflects our intense high-altitude light and slows water loss, which is why this is a plant that enjoys a Boulder summer rather than merely surviving it.[3]
care.planting: Plant out in spring once the soil has warmed, or in early fall to let roots settle before freeze-up; on the Front Range mid-May (after the average last frost) and early September are the two easy windows.[4] Set the crown at soil level — burying it in mulch invites crown rot. In containers it is easy and drought-proof, but a pot dries and freezes far faster than open ground: use a gritty, fast-draining mix, and either sink the pot or move it against a wall for winter, since roots in a pot are much less cold-hardy than the zone rating suggests.[1]
care.sun: Full sun gives the densest, most compact mat.[1][2] It will take light shade and even appreciates afternoon shade in the hottest exposures, but too much shade makes it stretch, thin out and hold moisture in the foliage, which is exactly what brings on leaf disease.[1]
care.soil: Average to lean, well-drained soil is all it asks, and it is markedly more adaptable than the species — it tolerates heavy clay, which is a real advantage on Front Range soils.[2] It is happy across a wide pH band from mildly acidic to our typical alkaline clay (roughly pH 6.0–7.8).[1][2] Sharp drainage matters far more than fertility; do not plant it in a low spot that stays wet.
care.water: Drought tolerant once established — water it in through the first season, then only during long dry spells.[2] Overwatering is the single most common way to kill it.[1] Water at the base with a drip line or wand: the woolly leaves hold overhead water against the crown, and that trapped moisture is what causes rot and leaf spot.[1] Good airflow between plants matters as much as the watering can.[1]
care.spacing: Space plants 12–18 in apart for groundcover use; they will close the gaps by runner within a season or two.[1] Leave a little more room in a still, enclosed bed so air can move through the foliage.[1]
care.propagation: Division is the standard method and the only way to keep the cultivar true — named clones will not come true from seed, and this one rarely sets any.[2] Lift and split clumps in spring or fall, pulling off rooted sections from the outside of the mat; the stems root freely wherever they touch soil, so rooted pieces are easy to find.[2] Divide every 4–5 years to rejuvenate a clump that has gone woody or bare in the middle.[2]
care.feeding: Do not feed it. Lamb's ear looks its best in lean soil, and fertilizer produces soft, floppy growth that is more prone to rot.[2]
care.maintenance: Genuinely low-maintenance.[1][2] Rake or comb out the dead, matted foliage in early spring before new growth pushes through — this is the one job that makes the difference between a handsome carpet and a grey mess. Snip off the occasional flower spike if one appears, to keep the foliage carpet unbroken.[2] Pull back any mulch that has crept over the crowns. Divide every few years when the centre thins.[2]
care.troubles: Rot and leaf disease in wet or humid conditions are the only real problems, and this cultivar resists them noticeably better than the species and most other selections — it is a specifically recommended choice where humidity defeats ordinary lamb's ear.[1] Well-drained soil is essential.[1] Root and crown rot follow wet soil, not cold.[2] The other thing to watch is vigour: it can spread aggressively by runner, so give it an edge to run into or expect to pull it back from its neighbours each spring.[1]
care.companions: A classic silver foil for roses, bearded iris, catmint and sedums, and it works in Mediterranean and rock gardens, moon or white gardens, and sensory gardens where the leaves get touched.[2] The oversized leaves also cut well for fresh and dried arrangements.[2]

edible.summary: Grown purely for its foliage — no part of lamb's ear is used as food.[1][3]
edible.caution: 'Big Ears' lamb's ear is an ornamental groundcover, not a food or herb plant, and no part of it should be eaten. It is not known to be poisonous — the species is not listed as toxic to people, dogs, cats or horses, and children brushing or handling the soft leaves is not a concern[3] — but 'not poisonous' is not the same as 'edible', and there is no documented culinary use for the leaves, flowers or roots.[1][3] The soft absorbent leaves of lamb's ear have a long folk-medicinal history as a field dressing for cuts, which is sometimes mistaken for a food use; it is not one. Do not confuse this plant with the culinary mint-family herbs it superficially resembles.
